title: How to Use Roth Conversions to Reduce RMDs Later
description: Strategic tax planning to defuse the Age 73 tax bomb.
content:
Traditional IRAs and 401(k)s are a ticking tax time bomb. At age 73, the IRS forces you to start withdrawing money (Required Minimum Distributions, or RMDs), whether you need it or not. These withdrawals count as ordinary income, potentially pushing you into a higher tax bracket and triggering Medicare surcharges (IRMAA). The solution is to proactively move money from Traditional to Roth accounts before age 73. This 'Roth Conversion' strategy pays taxes now (on your terms) to avoid forced taxes later.

Key Takeaways

  • The 'Tax Valley': The years between retirement (e.g., 60) and Social Security/RMDs (70/73) are the golden window. Your income is low. Use this time to convert Traditional balances to Roth at the 10% or 12% tax bracket.
  • Bracket Filling: Don't convert everything at once. Convert just enough to fill up your current tax bracket without jumping to the next one. This minimizes the effective tax rate.
  • RMD Reduction: Every dollar moved to Roth is a dollar that never faces RMDs. Reducing your Traditional balance to zero eliminates RMDs entirely.
  • Legacy Value: Roth IRAs are the best asset to leave to heirs because they are inherited tax-free. Traditional IRAs create a tax burden for your children.

Why It Matters (US Context)

Under the TCJA, tax rates are historically low until 2026. Converting now locks in these low rates before they potentially revert higher. This is a time-sensitive strategy.

The Conversion Math

Scenario: Couple Age 62. $1M Traditional IRA.

Option A: Do Nothing

At age 73, the IRA grows to $2M.
RMD (Year 1): ~$75,000.
Tax Impact: Added to Social Security, their taxable income spikes to $120k+. They pay 22% tax + potential IRMAA.

Option B: Systematic Conversion

From age 62 to 72 (10 years), they convert $50,000/year.
Tax Rate: They stay in the 12% bracket (income ~$80k).
Result: By age 73, the Traditional balance is small. RMDs are tiny. The bulk of the wealth is in Roth, growing tax-free.

The Verdict: Paying 12% voluntarily now saves paying 22%+ forcibly later.

Execution Steps

  1. November Review: Estimate your total income for the year. Calculate how much 'room' is left in the 12% or 22% bracket.
    Example: Income $50k. Top of bracket $94k. Room = $44k.
  2. Execute Trade: Transfer $44k from Traditional to Roth. Select 'Do Not Withhold Taxes'.
  3. Pay Tax with Cash: Write a check to the IRS using your savings account. Paying the tax from outside funds maximizes the amount inside the Roth.
  4. File Form 8606: Report the conversion on your taxes. It adds to your income for this year.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I convert too much?

Yes. If you convert $200k, you might hit the 32% bracket. That defeats the purpose. Only convert up to the 'cheap' brackets.

What about the 5-Year Rule?

Converted principal is penalty-free after 5 years. Since you are over 59.5, this is less of an issue for access, but the account needs to be open 5 years for earnings to be tax-free.

Does this affect Social Security tax?

Yes. A conversion increases your AGI for that year, which might make more of your Social Security taxable that year. Run the numbers to ensure the trade-off is worth it.
